frame.objective: Determine whether Neumann should create a differentiated proposition for home-studio creators and other individual buyers beyond its existing professional studio offering, or maintain a single professional range for all customers, based on evidence of market demand, current individual buyer reach, and potential value capture.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Must consider the Sennheiser group's broader strategic context and Neumann's existing product portfolio.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning for home‑studio creators and individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated proposition for home‑studio creators and individual buyers (e.g., entry‑level products, new branding, or separate sales channels).
2) Keep one professional range for all customers (no differentiation).
3) No expansion: maintain current product mix and focus on professional market.
4) Alternative: introduce a new professional‑grade product line for home‑studio creators while keeping existing professional offerings unchanged.

T1.claim: Home-studio creators and individual buyers will adopt premium professional-grade equipment if they perceive it as a status signal and a gateway to professional-level results, because they value credibility and quality that signals expertise.
T1.who_benefits: Neumann benefits by capturing higher-margin sales to creators who view gear as a credential and are willing to pay for perceived prestige.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Creators shift from entry-level to professional-grade gear when they believe it will elevate their work and attract professional opportunities (e.g., collaborations, paid projects).
T1.how_value_is_captured: Neumann can price premium products at higher rates and sell through dedicated channels (e.g., online store, creator-focused bundles) while leveraging the brand's reputation for professional quality.
assumptions: Creators associate professional-grade equipment with higher-quality sound and credibility.
Status signaling is a primary driver of purchase decisions for creators.
Neumann can communicate the prestige value effectively to creators.
predictions: Creators will express willingness to pay at least 20% more for professional-grade microphones compared to entry-level alternatives.
Searches for "Neumann professional studio" will be higher among creators than among general consumers.

X1.name: Creator Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated product pages and willingness-to-pay questions. Participants are recruited from a panel of home-studio creators (e.g., YouTubers, podcasters, independent musicians). Each participant views two product pages: a professional-grade microphone page emphasizing prestige and status (e.g., "The Neumann TLM102: the choice of top professionals for studio recording"); and a second page emphasizing performance metrics (e.g., "Neumann TLM102: 15% more sensitive, 20Hz‑20kHz flat response"). They are asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay for each page. The test also collects demographic data (e.g., years of experience, current gear).
X1.sample: 200 creators (100 per page) recruited via creator platforms and social media. Stratify by experience level (entry, intermediate, advanced) to capture a range of purchase behaviors.
X1.measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) difference between prestige and performance pages. Secondary measures: self‑reported importance of prestige vs. performance, and actual purchase intent (binary).

prediction_by_theory.T1: WTP for prestige page will be at least 20% higher than for performance page (i.e., prestige drives higher price).
prediction_by_theory.T2: WTP for performance page will be at least 20% higher than for prestige page (i.e., performance drives higher price).

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in average WTP between prestige and performance pages exceeds 20%, proceed to develop a differentiated proposition aligned with the higher‑value theory. If the difference is below 20%, maintain a single professional range for all customers.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address creator purchase drivers (prestige vs. performance). Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed Creator Purchase Intent Test (200 creators, two simulated product pages) to measure willingness-to-pay differences. If the prestige page yields at least a 20% higher WTP than the performance page, develop a differentiated proposition for home-studio creators and individual buyers; otherwise, maintain a single professional range for all customers.
final.target_customer: Home-studio creators and individual buyers who purchase professional-grade audio equipment for personal studio use.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated proposition that emphasizes prestige and status signaling, positioning Neumann as the choice of top professionals, and offering creator-focused bundles, tutorials, and community engagement to drive higher-margin sales.
final.next_action: Execute the Creator Purchase Intent Test (200 creators, two simulated product pages) within the 12‑week timeframe and €18,000 budget.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on creator purchase drivers. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows the performance page yields at least a 20% higher WTP, we would shift to a performance‑focused proposition and abandon prestige messaging.
If the test shows no significant difference or the prestige page outperforms, we would maintain a single professional range for all customers.

arguments.name: Creator Purchase Intent Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated product pages and willingness-to-pay questions. Participants are recruited from a panel of home-studio creators (e.g., YouTubers, podcasters, independent musicians). Each participant views two product pages: a professional-grade microphone page emphasizing prestige and status (e.g., "The Neumann TLM102: the choice of top professionals for studio recording"); and a second page emphasizing performance metrics (e.g., "Neumann TLM102: 15% more sensitive, 20Hz‑20kHz flat response"). They are asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay for each page. The test also collects demographic data (e.g., years of experience, current gear).
arguments.sample: 200 creators (100 per page) recruited via creator platforms and social media. Stratify by experience level (entry, intermediate, advanced) to capture a range of purchase behaviors.
arguments.measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) difference between prestige and performance pages. Secondary measures: self‑reported importance of prestige vs. performance, and actual purchase intent (binary).

prediction_by_theory.T1: WTP for prestige page will be at least 20% higher than for performance page (i.e., prestige drives higher price).
prediction_by_theory.T2: WTP for performance page will be at least 20% higher than for prestige page (i.e., performance drives higher price).

arguments.decision_rule: If the difference in average WTP between prestige and performance pages exceeds 20%, proceed to develop a differentiated proposition aligned with the higher‑value theory. If the difference is below 20%, maintain a single professional range for all customers.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence that a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, built on Jotun’s marine and protective coatings technology, would generate demand and justify investment, based on publicly available information known by mid‑2024.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence that a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, built on Jotun’s marine and protective coatings technology, would generate demand and justify investment, based on publicly available information known by mid‑2024.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home boat owners, DIY protective coatings) using Jotun’s marine/protective coatings.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence that a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, built on Jotun’s marine and protective coatings technology, would generate demand and justify investment, based on publicly available information known by mid‑2024.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence that a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, built on Jotun’s marine and protective coatings technology, would generate demand and justify investment, based on publicly available information known by mid‑2024.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid‑2024; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Jotun’s current B2B focus and unknown consumer reach.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to consumers for a specific use case.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home boat owners, DIY protective coatings) using Jotun’s marine/protective coatings.
2) Expand into consumer markets without differentiation, offering existing marine coatings directly to individual buyers through new distribution channels.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on B2B marine, protective, and powder coatings for shipyards, ship owners, infrastructure, and industry.
4) License Jotun’s technology to third‑party consumer brands for co‑branded products, leveraging existing consumer distribution.
5) Form strategic partnerships with consumer retailers or DIY chains to co‑brand and distribute Jotun’s consumer‑focused coatings.

T1.claim: Home boat owners will adopt Jotun marine coatings if they perceive the brand as a premium, reliable marine solution that meets regulatory requirements for biofouling and non-toxicity, and if they trust the brand’s technical expertise.
T1.who_benefits: Jotun gains premium pricing and brand loyalty from DIY and home boat owners who value marine performance and compliance.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Owners switch from generic or illegal paints to Jotun because they understand biofouling risks and want a brand that signals compliance and quality.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Jotun can charge higher margins on marine coatings and build a consumer brand that can be extended to other protective coatings, leveraging its existing distribution network.
assumptions: Home boat owners are aware of biofouling regulations and the risks of using prohibited paints.
Jotun’s marine coatings are perceived as the most reliable solution for regulatory compliance.
DIY consumers are willing to pay a premium for a brand they trust for marine performance.
predictions: If offered a Jotun marine coating at a 15% premium over generic paints, at least 30% of surveyed home boat owners will indicate intent to purchase.
Owners who have used Jotun for professional marine work will be more likely to purchase for home boats than those who have not.
T1.first_claim: Home boat owners will adopt Jotun marine coatings if they perceive the brand as a premium, reliable marine solution that meets regulatory requirements for biofouling and non-toxicity, and if they trust the brand’s technical expertise.

T2.claim: Home boat owners will adopt Jotun marine coatings if they seek a brand that offers DIY convenience, easy application, and fast curing times, because they value time‑saving and low‑maintenance solutions for home boat maintenance.
T2.who_benefits: Jotun gains volume sales through broader consumer reach and can price at a premium for convenience features, leveraging its existing distribution network.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Owners switch from professional‑grade coatings that require skilled application to Jotun marine coatings that are marketed as "do‑it‑yourself" and "fast cure", reducing installation effort and downtime.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Jotun can capture value through higher per‑unit margins on consumer‑oriented marine coatings and by bundling accessories or application kits, expanding its consumer presence beyond B2B marine.
assumptions: Home boat owners prioritize ease of application and fast curing times over other marine performance criteria.
Jotun can market marine coatings as DIY‑friendly without compromising marine performance.
DIY consumers are willing to pay a premium for convenience in marine coatings.
predictions: If offered a Jotun marine coating marketed as "DIY Fast Cure" at a 10% premium over standard marine coatings, at least 25% of surveyed home boat owners will indicate intent to purchase.
Owners who have used Jotun for professional marine work will be less likely to purchase for home boats than those who have not, because they expect professional‑grade performance.
T2.first_claim: Home boat owners will adopt Jotun marine coatings if they seek a brand that offers DIY convenience, easy application, and fast curing times, because they value time‑saving and low‑maintenance solutions for home boat maintenance.

X1.name: Home Boat Owner Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging
X1.sample: 500 home boat owners recruited via marine forums and social media, balanced across Scandinavia and other WESCA regions
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1‑Very unlikely to 7‑Very likely) and willingness to pay premium (percentage premium over generic marine paint). Secondary measure: self‑reported importance of biofouling compliance (1‑Not important to 7‑Very important).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Owners exposed to biofouling‑compliant messaging will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a 15% premium than those exposed to DIY‑convenience messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Owners exposed to DIY‑convenience messaging will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a 10% premium than those exposed to biofouling‑compliant messaging.

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two messaging groups exceeds 1.5 points on the 7‑point scale (e.g., compliance group at 5.5, convenience group at 4), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition aligned with the higher‑scoring

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing errors and does not address consumer demand, regulatory compliance, or DIY convenience. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed Home Boat Owner Purchase Intent Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent and willingness to pay for biofouling‑compliant versus DIY‑convenience messaging. If the test shows a ≥1.5‑point difference in purchase intent in favor of compliance messaging, develop a differentiated consumer proposition for home boat owners that emphasizes regulatory compliance and premium marine performance. If not,
final.target_customer: Home boat owners in Scandinavia and WESCA who currently use marine coatings for personal boats.
final.value_proposition: A Jotun marine coating marketed as a premium, biofouling‑compliant solution for home boats, leveraging the company’s existing distribution network and brand trust to capture higher margins and build a consumer brand.
final.next_action: Execute the 10‑week, €18,000 online survey test (X1) with 500 home boat owners, randomizing messaging and measuring purchase intent and willingness to pay.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand for compliance or convenience messaging. The test is needed to resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows a ≥1.5‑point advantage for compliance messaging, shift focus to T1 and develop a differentiated compliance‑focused proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference or a convenience advantage, reconsider expansion or license Jotun technology to third‑party consumer brands.

T1.claim: Health‑conscious consumers will purchase a stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser for home use because they value accurate body‑composition data and are willing to pay a premium for a device that provides reliable, professional‑grade results.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking to monitor health and body composition; Tanita benefits by capturing premium pricing and brand loyalty.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing public awareness of the health risks of excess body fat and the desire for precise, non‑invasive measurement motivates consumers to adopt home‑use devices.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can charge a higher price for a consumer version, leveraging its existing professional credibility and the perceived accuracy of the technology.
assumptions: Consumers trust professional‑grade devices for personal use.
Price sensitivity is low for health‑focused consumers.
Marketing can effectively communicate the device’s accuracy and benefits.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 15% above the price of standard consumer scales for a Tanita body‑fat analyser.
Purchase intent will be higher among those who have used professional body‑fat analyzers or have a history of health monitoring.

T2.claim: Consumers will purchase a stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser for home use because they seek convenience and privacy, and are willing to pay for a device that provides quick, non‑invasive results without needing a clinic visit.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing demand for at‑home health monitoring and the convenience of a stand‑up device that delivers results instantly motivates consumers to adopt home‑use devices.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can sell a consumer version at a lower price point than professional models, leveraging economies of scale and brand awareness to achieve volume sales and margin.
assumptions: Consumers prioritize speed and convenience over accuracy for body‑fat measurement.

predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay up to 20% less than the price of professional models for a comparable home device.

X1.sample: 500 adults aged 18-65 in the United States, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and income.
X1.measure: Average WTP (EUR) and binary purchase intent (yes/no). Secondary measures: perceived accuracy (1-10 scale) and perceived privacy (1-10 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average WTP ≥ 15% above the price of a comparable consumer scale (e.g., €120) and purchase intent ≥ 30%.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average WTP ≤ 20% below the price of a comparable consumer scale and purchase intent ≥ 30%.

X1.decision_rule: If average WTP is ≥ 15% above the baseline price AND purchase intent is ≥ 30%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition (supports T1). If average WTP is ≤ 20% below the baseline price AND purchase intent is ≥ 30%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition (supports T2).

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) to validate demand before committing resources. final.target_customer: Health‑conscious consumers who value accurate body‑composition data and are willing to pay a premium for professional‑grade results.
final.value_proposition: A stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyzer marketed as a professional‑grade home device, leveraging Tanita’s credibility and accuracy to capture premium pricing.
final.next_action: Run the willingness‑to‑pay survey (Test X1) within the €15,000 budget and 12‑week timeline.
final.uncertainty: Both demand (willingness to pay and purchase intent) and the competitive landscape (consumer market presence of competitors) remain uncertain.
would_change_if: If the survey shows average willingness to pay at least 15% above a comparable consumer scale and purchase intent of at least 30%, the case for a consumer proposition strengthens.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in 1993 to justify Tanita investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, originally launched for clinics and health clubs.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B clinic/health club market and any unknown consumer reach.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of reaching consumers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual home users with a stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser.
2) Expand the existing clinic/health club offering without differentiation (no new consumer proposition).
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and distribution channels.
4) License the technology to third parties for consumer applications.
5) Partner with retailers or fitness clubs to co‑brand a consumer version.

X1.name: Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Home Body-Fat Analyzer
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two price points: Price A (2.5x higher than existing home scales) and Price B (1.5x higher than existing home scales). Each participant views a product description emphasizing either clinical legitimacy (T1) or personal health monitoring (T2). They are asked: "Would you purchase this device at Price A?" (binary yes/no).
X1.sample: 500 Japanese adults aged 25-55, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and region.
X1.measure: Purchase intent at Price A (binary) and self-reported willingness to pay (WTP) in yen.

prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 40% of participants will indicate intent to purchase at Price A when the description emphasizes personal health monitoring.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in 1993 to justify Tanita investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser originally launched for clinics and health clubs.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to 1993; no internal company data.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home users with a stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in 1993 to justify Tanita investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, originally launched for clinics and health clubs.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B clinic/health club market and any unknown consumer reach.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of reaching consumers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual home users for self-monitoring of body composition.
2) Expand the existing clinic/health club offering without differentiation (no new consumer proposition).
3) Pursue a different route to consumers, such as partnering with retailers or offering a subscription service.
4) Target a different customer group, such as fitness enthusiasts or corporate wellness programs, using the same technology.
5) No expansion – maintain current focus on clinic/health club market.

T1.claim: Health‑conscious consumers will purchase a home body‑fat analyser because they self‑monitor body composition to track health and weight loss, and Tanita’s existing clinic/health club market demonstrates demand for accurate measurement.
T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers seeking to monitor health and weight; Tanita benefits by capturing premium home sales and building brand trust.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers increasingly view body composition as a health indicator; the Tanita device provides a convenient, accurate method to measure body fat without clinic visits.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita sells the device at a premium price directly to consumers, earning higher margins than clinic sales, and can leverage its existing brand trust to justify the price.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for accurate home body‑fat measurement.
Tanita’s clinic/health club reputation transfers to consumer perception of accuracy and reliability.
Distribution channels (e.g., retail) can reach consumers effectively in 1993.
predictions: If offered a home body‑fat analyser priced at a premium (e.g., $150–$200), at least 10% of surveyed health‑conscious adults will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales of the home device will be positively correlated with consumer awareness of Tanita’s clinic/health club body‑fat analyzers.

T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita sells the device at a premium price through retail channels, capturing higher margins than clinic sales and building brand awareness among consumers who value convenience.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay for home convenience and privacy in health monitoring.
Tanita’s clinic/health club reputation transfers to consumer perception of accuracy and reliability in home use.
Retail distribution can reach consumers effectively in 1993.
predictions: If offered a home body‑fat analyser priced at a premium (e.g., $150–$200) and marketed as a convenient, private tool, at least 8% of surveyed convenience‑seeking adults will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales of the home device will be inversely related to the perceived need for professional supervision, with higher purchase intent among those valuing self‑service.

X1.name: Home Body-Fat Analyzer Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two price points (premium: $150; standard: $75) and a brief description of the product (either health-monitoring focus or convenience/privacy focus). After reading the description, participants indicate whether they would purchase the device within 12 weeks on a 0‑10 scale. The test runs for 12 weeks, with 200 participants per group (total 400).
X1.sample: 400 health‑conscious adults (age 25–55) recruited via online panels in the United States.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (0‑10) for each price point and description.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium price group will show higher purchase intent than standard price group, regardless of description.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience‑focused description will generate higher purchase intent than health‑focused description, regardless of price.

X1.decision_rule: If premium price group’s average intent score is at least 5 points higher than standard price group, T1 is supported. If convenience description group’s average intent score is at least 5 points higher than health description group, T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or motivations for home use. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.target_customer: Individual health-conscious adults seeking home body composition monitoring
final.value_proposition: A premium home body-fat analyzer offering accurate, convenient measurement to support health monitoring
final.next_action: Conduct the proposed 12‑week online purchase intent test (400 participants, two price points, two description frames) to measure willingness to pay for a premium home device
final.uncertainty: Consumer demand for a premium home body-fat analyzer; willingness to pay a premium price; whether convenience or health motivation drives purchase intent; the feasibility of reaching consumers through retail channels in 1993
would_change_if: If the test shows premium price group purchase intent at least 5 points higher than standard price group, T1 would be supported and a consumer launch could be considered.
If a convenience‑focused description generates higher intent than a health‑focused description, T2 would be supported and a different marketing approach would be needed.
If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain and further testing would be required before any investment decision.

arguments.name: Home Body-Fat Analyzer Purchase Intent Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two price points (premium: $150; standard: $75) and a brief description of the product (either health-monitoring focus or convenience/privacy focus). After reading the description, participants indicate whether they would purchase the device within 12 weeks on a 0‑10 scale. The test runs for 12 weeks, with 200 participants per group (total 400).
arguments.sample: 400 health‑conscious adults (age 25–55) recruited via online panels in the United States.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (0‑10) for each price point and description.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium price group will show higher purchase intent than standard price group, regardless of description.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience‑focused description will generate higher purchase intent than health‑focused description, regardless of price.

arguments.decision_rule: If premium price group’s average intent score is at least 5 points higher than standard price group, T1 is supported. If convenience description group’s average intent score is at least 5 points higher than health description group, T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case leveraging its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) targeting individual buyers.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line without a new consumer proposition (status quo).
3) Pursue a different route to market or customer group (e.g., partner with outdoor retailers, target emergency preparedness organizations) while retaining the core technology.
4) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing markets.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they view them as a safety necessity for remote activities, and they are willing to pay a premium for a product that signals distress to search and rescue.
T1.who_benefits: Individual outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, kayakers) who need reliable emergency communication in remote areas.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing awareness of remote-area risks and a willingness to invest in safety equipment that can save lives.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell premium-priced distress beacons directly to consumers, capturing higher margins than bulk B2B sales.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in 2002 were sufficient to create a market for distress beacons.
Consumers associate 406 MHz beacons with life-saving capability.
Price sensitivity is low for a safety-critical product.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreationists will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price above $300.
Sales of ACR’s consumer-oriented distress beacon will be positively correlated with outdoor recreation participation rates in regions where it is marketed.
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they view them as a safety necessity for remote activities, and they are willing to pay a premium for a product that signals distress to search and rescue.

T2.claim: Emergency preparedness organizations (e.g., search and rescue teams, outdoor clubs) will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they require reliable, interoperable communication for remote operations, and they are willing to purchase specialized equipment that meets safety standards.
T2.who_benefits: Emergency preparedness organizations (SAR teams, outdoor clubs, government agencies) that need reliable distress communication in remote areas.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing recognition of the need for standardized, high-reliability communication for search and rescue, and a willingness to invest in equipment that meets regulatory requirements.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell bulk or subscription-based distress beacons to organizations, capturing volume sales and recurring revenue from maintenance contracts.
assumptions: Emergency preparedness organizations have a budget for specialized safety equipment.
Interoperability between different distress beacon systems is a critical purchase criterion.
Regulatory compliance (e.g., 406 MHz registration) is a prerequisite for procurement.
predictions: Emergency preparedness organizations will express intent to purchase 406 MHz distress beacons in quantities of at least 10 units.
Procurement decisions will be influenced by the ability of beacons to communicate with existing SAR networks.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case leveraging its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) targeting individual buyers.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line without creating a new consumer proposition (status quo).
3) Pursue a different route to market or customer group (e.g., partner with outdoor retailers, target emergency preparedness organizations) while retaining the core technology.
4) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing markets.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they view them as a safety necessity for remote travel, and are willing to pay a premium for a reliable, easy-to-use device that can be registered with NOAA.
T1.who_benefits: Individual outdoor recreationists (hikers, campers, climbers) who need emergency communication in remote areas.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Increased public awareness of remote-area hazards and the success of existing PLBs (e.g., ACR's GyPSI) creates a perception of necessity; registration requirement provides a clear regulatory pathway for use.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can charge premium prices for a consumer-friendly product, sell through outdoor retailers, and capture recurring registration fees and potential data services.
assumptions: Consumers perceive 406 MHz beacons as a critical safety tool for remote activities.
Retail distribution channels (outdoor stores) are willing to stock a dedicated consumer product.
Registration process is accessible and trusted by users.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreationists will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price above $300.
Sales through outdoor retailers will be positively correlated with the number of outdoor recreation events promoted in the same region.
Registration rates will exceed 50% of purchased units within six months of launch.
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they view them as a safety necessity for remote travel, and are willing to pay a premium for a reliable, easy-to-use device that can be registered with NOAA.

T2.claim: Emergency preparedness organizations (e.g., search-and-rescue teams, outdoor clubs) will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they require reliable, long-range communication for remote operations, and are willing to invest in a standardized, interoperable solution that can be integrated into existing SAR protocols.
T2.who_benefits: Emergency preparedness organizations (SAR teams, outdoor clubs, government agencies) that need reliable distress communication in remote areas.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing awareness of remote-area hazards and the success of existing PLBs create a need for standardized, high-reliability communication; regulatory requirements (e.g., NOAA registration) provide a clear framework for adoption.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell through B2B channels, offer volume discounts, and potentially capture data services (e.g., tracking, alert distribution) for emergency agencies.
assumptions: Emergency preparedness organizations prioritize reliable, long-range communication for remote operations.
Interoperability with existing SAR systems is a critical purchase criterion.
Organizational procurement cycles are influenced by regulatory alignment.
predictions: Surveyed emergency preparedness organizations will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price below $1,500 per unit.
Purchase decisions will be correlated with the presence of NOAA-compliant registration and interoperability testing.
Adoption rates will be higher in regions with active SAR operations and outdoor recreation activities.

X1.name: Consumer vs. Emergency Preparedness Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey experiment with two parallel groups receiving different product descriptions and price points.
X1.sample: 200 respondents: 100 outdoor recreation enthusiasts (recruited via outdoor activity forums) and 100 emergency preparedness organization members (recruited via SAR team and outdoor club mailing lists).
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would you buy this product?") and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor recreation group will show purchase intent ≥40% and WTP ≥$300; emergency preparedness group will show purchase intent <30% and WTP <$1,500.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Emergency preparedness group will show purchase intent ≥40% and WTP ≥$1,500; outdoor recreation group will show purchase intent <30% and WTP <$300.

X1.decision_rule: If outdoor recreation purchase intent ≥40% and WTP ≥$300, proceed with consumer product launch. If emergency preparedness purchase intent ≥40% and WTP ≥$1,500, pursue B2B/emergency agency sales. If neither condition met, recommend no expansion.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed consumer vs. emergency preparedness messaging test to validate demand before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hikers, campers, climbers) who need emergency communication in remote areas
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon that is easy to use, compatible with NOAA registration, and sold through outdoor retailers at a price justifying premium positioning.
final.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €18,000 online survey experiment with 200 respondents (100 outdoor recreation enthusiasts, 100 emergency preparedness organization members) to test purchase intent and willingness to pay for a consumer‑focused product.
final.uncertainty: Both demand for a consumer product and willingness to pay a premium price are unknown; the regulatory environment (registration, interoperability) is clear but market size and competitive landscape are not.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent ≥40% and willingness to pay ≥$300 for a consumer product, proceed with launch.
If the test shows purchase intent ≥40% and willingness to pay ≥$1,500 for an emergency preparedness product, pursue B2B/emergency agency sales.
If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case leveraging its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case leveraging its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) targeting individual buyers.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line without a new consumer proposition (status quo).
3) Pursue a different route to market or customer group (e.g., partner with outdoor retailers, target emergency preparedness organizations) while retaining the core technology.
4) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing markets.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing awareness of remote-area risks and a willingness to invest in safety equipment that can save lives.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell premium-priced distress beacons directly to consumers, capturing higher margins than bulk B2B sales.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in 2002 were sufficient to create a market for distress beacons.
Consumers associate 406 MHz beacons with safety and reliability.
Price sensitivity is low for a life-saving device.

Sales of ACR’s consumer-oriented distress beacon will be positively correlated with outdoor recreation participation rates in regions where it is marketed.
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they view them as a safety necessity for remote activities, and they are willing to pay a premium for a product that signals distress to search and rescue.

T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell bulk or subscription-based distress beacons to organizations, capturing volume sales and recurring revenue from maintenance contracts.
assumptions: Emergency preparedness organizations have a budget for specialized safety equipment.
Interoperability between different distress beacon systems is a critical purchase criterion.
Regulatory compliance (e.g., 406 MHz registration) is a prerequisite for procurement.
predictions: Emergency preparedness organizations will express intent to purchase 406 MHz distress beacons in quantities of at least 10 units.

X1.measure: Purchase intent: "Would you buy a 406 MHz distress beacon for yourself (outdoor recreation) or for your organization (SAR team/outdoor club) at a price of $350?" (binary: Yes/No)

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor recreationists will indicate intent to purchase for personal use at a rate above 30% (i.e., ≥30% Yes).

X1.decision_rule: If personal purchase intent ≥30% and organizational purchase intent ≥30%, both theories are supported. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Deere’s existing dealer network and current reach to individual buyers (unknown from dossier).
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home‑garden, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand into consumer markets without differentiation, offering tractors directly to individual buyers through dealers.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on farm, combine, and industrial equipment sales through dealers.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications (e.g., mobile equipment manufacturers).

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they view them as a convenient, time‑saving tool for yard work, and they are willing to purchase directly from Deere if the price is competitive with other brands.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking efficient yard care; Deere gains sales and brand recognition in the consumer market.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing suburban population and increasing disposable income make yard work a visible, time‑critical task; a tractor offers faster mowing than hand tools.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells tractors directly to consumers through dealers, capturing margin on each unit and building brand loyalty that can be leveraged for future sales.
assumptions: Suburban growth in the 1960s increases demand for yard care.
Consumers perceive lawn tractors as a status symbol and are willing to pay a premium.
Deere can produce tractors at scale and maintain quality comparable to competitors.
predictions: If Deere launches a consumer‑focused lawn tractor model, sales will exceed 1,000 units in the first year.
Consumer surveys will show willingness to pay a price 10% above comparable models from other brands.
Deere’s dealer network will be willing to stock the new model, indicating market acceptance.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they view them as a convenient, time‑saving tool for yard work, and they are willing to purchase directly from Deere if the price is competitive with other brands.

T2.claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they view them as a status symbol and a symbol of modern, comfortable living, and they are willing to purchase them even if the price is higher than functional alternatives.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking to signal wealth and modern lifestyle; Deere gains premium sales and brand prestige.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Post‑World War II affluence and suburban growth create a market segment that values lifestyle signaling and convenience; a tractor is seen as a modern, desirable tool.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells tractors at premium prices through dealers, capturing higher margins and building a brand associated with luxury and status.
assumptions: Affluent suburban homeowners prioritize status and lifestyle signaling in purchasing household goods.
Deere can position its tractors as premium, lifestyle products rather than purely functional tools.
Consumers are willing to pay a price premium for a brand associated with prestige.
predictions: If Deere launches a consumer‑focused lawn tractor model priced 20% above comparable models, early adopters will purchase at least 500 units in the first year.
Surveys will show that a majority of buyers cite status or prestige as a primary reason for purchasing.
Deere’s dealer network will be willing to allocate shelf space to the premium model, indicating market acceptance of a higher‑priced offering.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a lawn tractor (specifications, price, and a brief narrative emphasizing either convenience/time‑saving (for T1) or status/modern lifestyle (for T2). They then indicate whether they would purchase it and, if so, the maximum price they would pay. X1.sample: 200 U.S. adults aged 30‑65, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and region. Each participant sees only one narrative and is randomly assigned to either the convenience or status group.
X1.measure: Average maximum price willing to pay (EUR) and binary purchase intent (yes/no).

prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants exposed to the status narrative will show a higher average maximum price and higher purchase intent than those exposed to the convenience narrative.

final.target_customer: Homeowners in suburban areas who value time‑saving yard work and are willing to purchase directly from Deere if the price is competitive with other brands.
final.value_proposition: A lawn tractor positioned as a convenient, time‑saving tool for yard care, sold directly to consumers through existing dealer network, leveraging Deere’s engineering and brand reputation to capture margin.
final.next_action: Run the proposed consumer preference test (200 U.S. adults, 10 weeks, €15,000) to measure willingness to pay for convenience messaging versus status messaging.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Deere’s existing dealer network and current reach to individual buyers (unknown from dossier).
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home‑garden, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand into consumer markets without differentiation, offering tractors directly to individual buyers through dealers.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on farm, combine, and industrial equipment sales through dealers.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications (e.g., mobile equipment manufacturers).

X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn Tractor Purchase
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a John Deere lawn tractor (specifications, price, and a brief description of its time‑saving benefits). They are then asked: "Would you purchase this tractor?" (Yes/No). A secondary question asks: "What is the most important factor influencing your decision?" (Time‑saving, status/lifestyle, price, or other).
X1.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners aged 25‑65 who have a yard and own a lawn mower (recruited via panel). Stratified by region to reflect 1962 demographic distribution.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and primary decision factor (categorical).

prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 35% of participants will indicate purchase intent and cite status/lifestyle as the primary factor, even if price is 20% higher than functional competitors.
